catalog_citation: Watahomigie, Lucille J., Jorigine Bender & Akira Y. Yamamoto. 1982. Hualapai Reference Grammar. Los Angeles: American Indian Studies Center, UCLA. (ERIC ED250132)
catalog_locator: section 2.3 Stress, pp. 39-40 (ERIC PDF pp. 61-62); suffix secondary-stress remark ca. p. 372 (PDF p. 394)
catalog_quote: 2.3 Stress. In the previous sections, we did not explain which part of a word is pronounced louder or higher. When a word contains two or more vowels, we often pronounce one part louder or higher than other parts. To tell us which part is louder or higher (that is, which part of the word is stressed or accented), we can use a stress mark over the vowel--the symbol (´) for the strong and the symbol (`) for the weaker accents. For example, the word for "horse" can be written as òló. This means, then, that we pronounce the word òló with the second o louder or higher. A general rule of the accent placement is as follows: When there are two or more vowels in a word and when one of them is a long vowel, the stress is usually placed on the long vowel. Examples are presented below: vàsú:k 'to be green', jigyó:k 'to bite', wàsí:vk 'to think'. [p.40] A long vowel, then, is usually stressed, there…

audit.recode_to: morphological (set by morphology): one primary stress per word on the root/stem vowel (root usually word-final or followed only by consonantal suffixes/unstressed -a,-i,-o and unstressed auxiliaries; prefixes unstressed). The vowel-length contrast lives on the stressed root vowel and plural/distributive morphology lengthens 'the stressed vowel of the stem', so WBY 1982's 'stress the long vowel' is a reading heuristic (surface corollary), not the mechanism. Edge: not-applicable; weight class: none. The not-fixed/not-initial correction against StressTyp2 (1L) and Gordon 2002 ('Initial') stands unchanged.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: verbatim at the stated pages in held page images (p.39-40 = PDF 61-62; suffix remark p.372 = PDF 394). (2) Deciding source: a 1982 community/pedagogical reference grammar (primary, linguist co-author, 575 pp, open) whose stress section is a hedged orthographic heuristic; it is not the best available description: a 2001 revised edition exists, and the specialist literature on this languoid (Redden 1966 Walapai phonology; Shaterian 1983/Thomas 1992 Yavapai; Berardo 1992 Hualapai-Havasupai; Langdon 1977 comparative) is unheld. (3) Three open items downloaded now all frame Upland Yuman stress as root stress: Berardo 1992:70 (Hualapai/Havasupai: stressed syllable = morphological root, 'the only part that carries inherent stress'), Thomas 1992:90 (Yavapai: 'Primary stress is always on the root') and 1992:91 quoting Redden 1966:8 (Hualapai: three stress phonemes, vowel length cond
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again: confirmed in the copy we hold. Held page images (book p.39 = ERIC PDF p.61) and -p.40 = PDF p.62) carry sec. 2.3 'Stress' verbatim: 'When there are two or more vowels in a word and when one of them is a long vowel, the stress is usually placed on the long vowel' with òló, vàsú:k, jìgyó:k, wàsí:vk (p.39) and 'A long vowel, then, is usually stressed, therefore in this book, the stress mark is not written on the long vowel', Banya:nyuwà, mùlvwayo:wo, thambó ~ thmbó (p.40). Suffix remark 'the suffix receives secondary stress or sometimes weak stress' verbatim on book

sources.quote: Yavapai (same glottocode): word = (c*)[cv(c)]root(c*)(v); 'The root vowel may have a vowel length contrast ... Primary stress is always on the root.' Quotes Redden 1966:8 on Hualapai: 'Vowel length is conditioned by the alternating-stress system, but phonetic vowel length has a very complex distribution ... There are three stress phonemes: primary, secondary, and weak', and reports Redden denies a phonemic length contrast in Pai altogether.

sources.quote: 'Words in Yuman languages typically consist of a monosyllabic, stress-bearing root ... Yuman languages regularly stress the final syllable of a word's root, which tends also to be word-final, and so words in Yuman languages typically exhibit word-final stress (Kroeber 1943; Langdon 1977a, 1977b; Wares 1968).' Hualapai loans truncate post-stress vowels to restore root/word-final stress (aʔíːl 'thread', taméts 'tomatoes', kǽnɾi 'candy').

sources.quote: 'the stressed syllable of the Yuman word coincides with the morphological root, which typically has the shape of CVC but can also be CV, VC, or V. The root can be considered "the indispensable phonological and semantic core of the word, the only part that carries inherent stress" (Langdon 1976:221). ... Redden 1966 sites eighteen different root shapes.' Hualapai/Havasupai allophones of /r/, /l/, /q/ are conditioned by position relative to the primary-stressed (root) syllable.
sources.locator: p.70, 'The Structure of the Yuman Word'; allophony sections pp.65-73 organised by pre-/post-stress position
